tier_reason: soumith/convnet-benchmarks is a well-known independent third-party suite with public scripts (caffe/install.sh, caffe/run_imagenet.sh, torch7/imagenet_winners/benchmark.lua) and states CPU model plus GPU (i7-5930K + Titan X), and its README tables show Caffe native ahead of Torch-7 native SpatialConvolutionMM on AlexNet 324 vs 342 ms, Overfeat 823 vs 878 ms and OxfordNet-A 1068 vs 1105 ms; compiler, flags and CUDA version are not stated, so not A.

corrections.caveats: Margin over Torch-7 native is only 3 to 7 percent, and both are im2col + cuBLAS GEMM fallback kernels (Torch's SpatialConvolutionMM follows the same approach), so the gap is within what separate runs on different dates can produce. The README Caffe rows cannot be traced to the checked-in logs: caffe/output_alexnet.log, output_overfeat.log, output_vgg_a.log and output_googlenet.log (dated Feb 28, build configuration not recorded) report Average Forward-Backward 128.7, 430.1, 680.2 and 484.7 ms, far below the README's Caffe rows of 324, 823, 1068 and 1935 ms, while the Torch nn row matches torch7/imagenet_winners/output_raw.log (339.72 ms, a May 2015 run); so the Caffe-vs-Torch comparison mixes runs from different dates. The same tables show Caffe (native) well behind TensorFlow (81 ms on AlexNet vs 324), cuDNN R4 through Torch bindings (81 ms), Nervana neon (87 ms), fbfft (104 ms), Chainer (177 ms) and cuda-convnet2 (177 ms), and on GoogleNet V1 Caffe is at 1935 ms against TensorFlow 445 ms, so Caffe is not faster than the modern baselines (TensorFlow, PyTorch, cuDNN). The README notes Caffe (native) and Torch (native) are only the default fallback kernels and that cuDNN can also be used through Caffe bindings; caffe/install.sh builds from Makefile.config.example with cuDNN disabled but states no compiler, flags or CUDA version. Benchmark is 2015-2016 era (cuDNN R2/R4, Titan X); Caffe has had no commit since 2020-02-13. The project's own paper (arXiv 1408.5093, 'over 40 million images a day on a K40', snippet only) was not reachable here (arxiv.org blocked) and gives no baseline numbers in the snippet.

notes: Numbers match the convnet-benchmarks README exactly; entry is real but marginal (3-7% over Torch-7 native, far slower than cuDNN/TensorFlow/neon). Shortcomings: README Caffe rows disagree with the repo's own checked-in Caffe logs (128.7 ms AlexNet vs 324 in the table), compiler/flags unstated, 2015-2016 hardware, abandoned since 2020-02-13. Metadata (BSD-2-Clause, 34.6k stars, last commit 2020-02-13, not archived) confirmed.

tier_reason: First-party notebook (catboost/benchmarks model_evaluation_speed/model_evaluation_benchmark.ipynb, with the three model files checked in) shows CatBoost 184 ms vs XGBoost 4.89 s and LightGBM 11.1 s at 32 threads and 1.98 s vs 1 min 12 s and 1 min 56 s at 1 thread, but states no CPU model, compiler, flags or library versions, so C.

corrections.hardware: Not stated for the prediction notebook (32 threads; Python 3.7.3 kernel). The training_speed README states Intel Xeon E312xx (Sandy Bridge) 32 cores for CPU runs and NVIDIA GTX1080TI + Intel Core i7-6800K for its GPU table; the 17.9 ms/tree GPU tree-construction comparison (gpu_vs_cpu_training_speed README) ran on an NVIDIA P100 with an Intel Xeon E5-2660 host.
corrections.caveats: First-party benchmark with a public notebook and checked-in model files, but the prediction notebook states no CPU model, compiler, flags or library versions (the catboost 0.10.3 / xgboost 0.80 / lightgbm 2.2.1 versions are listed only in the training_speed README; the notebook kernel is Python 3.7.3), so tier C. The models are comparable in size: LightGBM_model.txt holds about 14.8k trees with 64 leaves each, truncated to 8000 at predict time, matching CatBoost's 8000 depth-6 (64-leaf) symmetric trees; CatBoost's speed comes from oblivious-tree evaluation. The LightGBM predict call sets no thread count, and the XGBoost/LightGBM timings include their own input handling while the CatBoost Pool is built outside the timed cell. XGBoost and LightGBM have been optimised since 2018, so the ratio is probably smaller today. Independent training benchmark szilard/GBM-perf shows CatBoost slower than both on CPU (1M rows: CatBoost 7.0 s vs XGBoost 2.7 s and LightGBM 4.0 s; 10M rows: 70 s vs 40 s and 20 s) and slower than XGBoost on GPU (3.4 s vs 1.3 s on 1M rows); it does not test prediction. In the repo's own CPU training table CatBoost is also slower on letters (259.75 s vs XGBoost 176.82 s and LightGBM 112.74 s) and airline (974.1 s vs XGBoost 611.9 s and LightGBM 526.2 s). The benchmarks repo README contains no numbers; the model_evaluation_speed folder has no README.

notes: All prediction and training numbers verified in the notebook and the training_speed / gpu_vs_cpu_training_speed READMEs; ratios correct. Shortcomings: first-party, 2018-2019 library versions, no CPU model/compiler for the prediction run, CatBoost slower than XGBoost/LightGBM for training on several datasets and in szilard/GBM-perf. Metadata (Apache-2.0, 9.1k stars, last commit 2026-10-07) confirmed.

tier_reason: The numbers are in the archived 'Older results' tables of the first-party wiki page Indexing-1G-vectors (Bigann run with benchs/bench_polysemous_1bn.py), which compare against figures copied from two CVPR'16 papers on other hardware and state no compiler, flags or CPU model, so C; the peer-reviewed GPU paper (arXiv 1702.08734) reports the 8.5x win over Wieschollek et al. but could only be read as a search snippet here.

corrections.hardware: Archived comparison tables: Faiss rows on 'CPU (1 thread)', 'CPU (20 threads)', one Titan X, 4*K40 and 8*TitanX, CPU model not stated for these rows; baseline rows are the figures published in the 2016 papers on their own hardware (Titan X GPU; 1 CPU thread). The page's current bench_all_ivf experiments (no external baseline) ran on a 2.2 GHz Xeon E5-2698 (80 cores, 32 used).
corrections.caveats: The comparison sits in the wiki's archived 'Older results' section; the current results on that page compare only Faiss configurations with each other. The baselines are numbers copied from two 2016 papers, not rerun on the same machine, and are research code rather than a library, so the ratios compare across different hardware; the Bigann CPU rows compare Faiss on a CPU against a GPU baseline, and Faiss on 1 CPU thread (0.4852 ms/vector at R@10 0.349) is about 3.2x slower than Wieschollek et al. on a Titan X (0.15 ms) (derived from page data). The wiki's Titan X row (0.0340 ms at R@10 0.376) differs from the GPU paper's 17.7 microseconds at the same recall (snippet only), which is where the README's 8.5x 'fastest GPU kNN' claim comes from. Compiler and flags are not stated (last_commit is the v1.15.1 release date from CHANGELOG.md, which also has an Unreleased section; the commit-list page returned HTTP 429). The Indexing-1M-vectors wiki page shows a library baseline beating Faiss: on SIFT1M nmslib HNSW takes 0.081 s at 1-R@1 0.8195 vs Faiss IVF16384,Flat 0.538 s at 0.8980 on CPU (the page says nmslib is faster but uses more memory; machines differ between tables). The wiki's FastScan-vs-ScaNN 1.1.1 comparison (1 thread, Xeon E5-2698) is only plotted in images and says 'faster and more accurate for all operating points before re-ranking' on SIFT1M, so no numbers were read; its '280k vs 140k QPS' HNSW comparison is against Faiss's own HNSW. The GPU paper (arXiv 1702.08734) could not be opened here (arxiv.org, ar5iv and deepai blocked); a paper-access retier could move this entry to B.

notes: Deep1B (3.66 vs 20 ms, 5.5x) and Bigann (0.035 / 0.0340 vs 0.15 ms, 4.3x / 4.4x) numbers verified in the archived tables of the 1G wiki page; nmslib caveat verified on the 1M page. Shortcomings: cross-hardware comparison against figures copied from 2016 papers, archived results, no compiler/flags/CPU model for the compared rows, nmslib faster on SIFT1M; candidate for a paper-access retier to B via the GPU paper (8.5x over Wieschollek et al., snippet only). Metadata (MIT, 41.1k stars, not archived) confirmed; last commit date not checkable (HTTP 429 twice).
